R12 (reworded), the small emphasis words he adds when he reads.
- 'actually': put it on the turn of the piece. verdict.why:
The core of the rule holds: he says figures as written when they sit in plain lines, and they drift where he riffs. But the stated mechanism and the test are wrong in four ways.

(a) The rule misses the most common drift: the prediction deadline. He rounded it in all 4 takes that gave a day or month (31 December became 'the end of December' twice, 30 June became 'middle of', 'end of June' became 'mid-'). He also hedged the odds in 2 takes. The rule's advice to keep facts away from riff turns can't cover this, because the prediction is always a riff turn and has to carry the date and odds.

(b) Sentence length and starting with the subject don't decide whether a fact survives. Long fact lines came through word for word, and short subject-first lines were lost or added to. The 12-word guide is a fair rule of thumb for lines in general, not a test for facts.

(c) The worked 'after' example breaks the rule itself. Its first line is 13 words and starts 'Before,'; its second starts 'With the automatic picker,'. It also misses the cause: the 6-word 'After, seven in a hundred did.' was already short. It was lost because it was the second half of a contrast split over two lines, in a paragraph where he stopped to explain in his own words.

(d) The check would flag good lines and clashes with house rules. 'Starts with a pronoun' flags every 'I'm N% sure.' odds line, which is the house prediction format. 'Over 12 words with says/said' flags the Altman lines he said word for word. Splitting each figure into its own sentence can also produce bare scores unless the scale stays in the same sentence, as PLAIN_SCORES requires.

The rule fits the other house rules: short plain lines, reading age 12, one line of thought, analogies untouched. Its one risk is a run of flat fact lines tipping into newsreader delivery, so the fact lines should sit inside his reflective framing.

This is not a transcriber artefact. The drifts that count are whole phrases, and the lone dropped word is flagged in the counts above.
verdict.corrected_rule:
R13 (reworded): Write each must-say fact, figure, name and source as one plain line that carries the whole fact: the number, its unit, and for any score its scale and what it is compared with, in the same sentence (PLAIN_SCORES). Keep it out of the lines he riffs on: the opening set-up, the turn into the prediction, and the line straight after a point he is likely to explain in his own words.
- Put a before-and-after or two-figure contrast in one sentence, or lead with the figure that must be said ('Seven in a hundred free users then used thinking each day, up from under one.'). He merges two-line contrasts and drops the second half.
- In the prediction, put the deadline and the odds in their own short lines. Write the deadline as a month, the way he says it ('by the end of December 2027'), never a day number. He turned 31 December into 'the end of December' and 30 June into 'the middle of'.
- Lines of about 12 words or fewer are kept word for word most often. Use that as guidance for every line, not as the test for facts.

Check: flag a must-say figure that shares its sentence with an aside, a 'which' clause or a second figure; a contrast split across two sentences; a deadline written as a day number; and a score without its scale. After each take, check every fact-gate figure, name, and the call's deadline and odds against the words file. A fact he changed, or a new unchecked fact he added (such as 'ChatGPT is now also going into ads'), goes back to the fact gate or is cut before publishing.
